title: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
summary: Fit a model into a phone or microcontroller: size, RAM and latency budgets, affine int8 quantization, integer-only inference, per-channel and QAT, depthwise convolutions and pruning.
outcomes: Compute a model's flash size, peak activation memory and latency on a microcontroller from its shape
Compute the scale and zero point that quantize a tensor to int8 and bound the rounding error
Explain how an int8 layer runs with int32 accumulation and a fixed-point requantization multiplier
Choose between per-tensor and per-channel scales, static and dynamic calibration, and PTQ and QAT
Compute the MAC savings of depthwise separable convolution and when pruning actually saves space

lessons.title: The three budgets a model must fit on a small device

blocks.md: **Edge AI** means running a model's inference on the device that collects the data: a phone, a Raspberry Pi, or a microcontroller inside a sensor. Doing it locally removes the network round trip, works offline, saves bandwidth and cloud cost, and keeps raw data on the device. The catch is that the model was usually trained on a server with gigabytes of memory and a power budget of hundreds of watts.

How small is small? The TensorFlow Lite Micro paper (David et al., 2020) describes the range: a big embedded system has a few megabytes of flash ROM and at most a megabyte of SRAM, while a small one has a few hundred kilobytes or fewer, split between ROM and RAM. Such chips cost less than a few US dollars and may run on a few milliwatts, where phone and desktop CPUs draw watts.

blocks.title: Where a model lives on a microcontroller

scenes.caption: Three resources matter. Flash holds the model file and the program, SRAM holds the working tensors, and the CPU does the multiply-adds.
Storage budget: every weight sits in flash for the device's whole life, so model size in bytes must fit beside the code.
Working-memory budget: activations are written and read back during one inference. They need fast RAM, which is the scarcest resource.
Latency and energy budget: the number of multiply-adds and the bytes moved per inference set how long it takes and how much battery it costs.

blocks.md: **Storage** is the easy one to compute: parameters times bytes per parameter. A 32-bit float (fp32) takes 4 bytes; an 8-bit integer (int8) takes 1. Take a hypothetical model with 250,000 parameters (all sizes here use 1 KB = 1024 bytes).

scenes.caption: fp32: 250,000 x 4 bytes = 976.6 KB. On a chip with 1 MB of flash this leaves almost nothing for the program.
fp16 halves it to 488.3 KB. LiteRT documents float16 quantization as up to 50% smaller.
int8 stores one byte per weight: 244.1 KB, a 4x cut. This is the 'up to 75%' smaller in the LiteRT docs.
Prune 80% of weights, then store each survivor as an int8 value plus an 8-bit position gap: 50,000 x 2 bytes = 97.7 KB, 10x below fp32. Simplified: ignores the small per-layer metadata.

blocks.md: **Working memory** is subtler. Activations do not all live at once: a tensor is needed only from the operator that writes it until the last operator that reads it. The MobileNetV2 paper (Sandler et al., 2018) writes the memory needed by a chain-structured network as the largest combined input plus output size over all operators:

blocks.caption: |op| is any scratch memory the operator itself needs. Weights are excluded: they stay in flash.

blocks.title: Peak activation memory of a toy int8 network (KB)

scenes.caption: A 96x96x1 int8 image goes through a conv (stride 2, 8 channels), depthwise and pointwise layers, pooling and a 2-class output. Each cell is that operator's input plus output in KB.
The pointwise layer that turns a 48x48x8 tensor into 48x48x16 needs 18 + 36 = 54 KB at once. That is the peak.
Keeping every activation alive would need 108 KB. Reusing buffers whose lifetimes do not overlap needs only 54 KB, which is what TFLM's memory planner does inside one fixed arena.

blocks.md: **Latency** on a microcontroller is roughly cycles divided by clock rate. The TFLM paper ran the Visual Wake Words person detector on an Arm Cortex-M4 at 96 MHz: 18,990.8K cycles with reference kernels (197.8 ms) and 4,857.7K cycles with the optimized CMSIS-NN kernels (50.6 ms). **Energy** is dominated by moving data: Han et al. (2016) cite, for 45 nm CMOS, 0.9 pJ for a 32-bit float add, 5 pJ for a 32-bit SRAM read and 640 pJ for a 32-bit DRAM read, so fewer and smaller bytes save battery directly.

The toolbox for fitting these budgets has four tools, and this course covers them in order of how often they are used: **quantization** (fewer bits per number), **efficient architectures** (fewer multiply-adds per layer), **pruning** (fewer weights) and **distillation**. You already know distillation: train a small student on a large teacher's temperature-softened outputs plus the true labels. In edge work it usually produces the small float model that the other three tools then compress.

A model fits a device only if three numbers fit: bytes of weights versus flash, peak bytes of live activations versus RAM, and cycles per inference versus the latency target. Check all three before training anything.

blocks.question: A model has 250,000 int8 weights (244 KB) and its largest operator reads a 40 KB tensor and writes a 40 KB tensor. The target has 256 KB of flash and 64 KB of SRAM. What is the problem?
options: Nothing, both fit
The weights do not fit in flash
The peak activations (80 KB) do not fit in SRAM
The model must be fp32 to run on a CPU
blocks.explain: Weights live in flash: 244 KB is under 256 KB, though tight once code is added. Activations need the peak of input plus output, 80 KB, which is more than 64 KB of SRAM. You would shrink the largest feature map (fewer channels or lower resolution), not the weights.

blocks.question: Two candidate models have the same parameter count. Model B has half the multiply-adds but twice the peak activation size. On a battery sensor with very little SRAM, which statement is right?
options: B is always better because it does less arithmetic
Parameter count alone decides, so they are equivalent
B may not run at all, because peak activation memory is a separate hard limit
A is always better because activations dominate energy
blocks.explain: Parameters, multiply-adds and peak activation memory are three independent budgets. If B's peak activations exceed the arena, it cannot run no matter how few operations it has.

lessons.title: Affine quantization: storing reals as int8 plus a scale

blocks.md: A trained layer's weights are real numbers in a narrow range, for example between -0.62 and 0.95. Spending 32 bits on each is wasteful: 8 bits give 256 levels, and if we spread those levels evenly across the range actually used, each weight is off by at most half a step.

Jacob et al. (2018), the scheme adopted by TensorFlow Lite, define this as an **affine map** from an integer $q$ to a real $r$ with two constants per array: a **scale** $S$ (a positive real, the step size) and a **zero point** $Z$ (an integer, the code that stands for real 0).

blocks.caption: Equation 1 of Jacob et al. One (S, Z) pair is shared by a whole weight or activation array.

blocks.tex: S = \frac{r_{max} - r_{min}}{q_{max} - q_{min}}, \qquad Z = \mathrm{round}\Big(q_{min} - \frac{r_{min}}{S}\Big), \qquad q = \mathrm{clamp}\big(\mathrm{round}(r/S) + Z,\ q_{min},\ q_{max}\big)
blocks.caption: For int8, q_min = -128 and q_max = 127. The range is first widened to include 0 so that Z is a valid code.

blocks.md: Why insist that 0 is exactly representable? Convolutions pad borders with zeros, and ReLU produces many exact zeros. If 0 landed between two levels, every padded pixel would carry a small bias. Choosing $Z$ as the integer code for 0 makes real 0 round-trip with no error.

scenes.caption: Divide by S and add Z. The ends land near -128 and 127, and real 0 lands exactly on -27.
Round to the nearest integer and clamp to [-128, 127]. These six bytes plus (S, Z) are what gets stored.
Dequantize with S(q - Z). The values come back close but not equal.
Every error is below S/2 = 0.0031 (the largest is 0.0023), and 0 is exact. Rounding error is bounded by half a step for any value inside the range.

blocks.prompt: Now replace the largest weight 0.95 with an outlier, 9.5, and requantize all six. What happens to the error on the other five weights?
blocks.reveal: The range becomes [-0.62, 9.5], so S grows 6.4x to 0.0397 and Z becomes -112. The five ordinary weights now map to codes -128, -117, -112, -110 and -104: they share a handful of levels, and their worst error rises from 0.0023 to 0.0184, about 8x. One outlier coarsens the grid for every value in the array. This is why calibration methods often clip rare extremes (percentile or entropy calibration) instead of using the raw min and max.

blocks.md: A common simplification is the **symmetric** quantizer: force $Z = 0$ and set $S = \max|r| / 127$. LiteRT stores weights this way, as int8 in [-127, 127] with zero point 0, while activations keep an asymmetric zero point. Symmetric is cheaper in the integer math (next lesson) but wastes levels when the range is lopsided: for our six weights $S = 0.95/127 = 0.00748$, the codes run from -83 to 127, and codes -127 to -84 are never used. The worst error grows from 0.0023 to 0.0033.

blocks.title: Worst-case rounding error versus bit width

scenes.caption: With range 1.57 (our six weights), 8 bits give a worst error of 0.0031. Each extra bit halves it.
With the outlier the range is 10.12: at 8 bits the worst error is about 0.02, larger than a typical small weight of 0.01. Those weights are effectively noise.
At 4 bits even the clean range has a step of 0.105 (worst error 0.052, the curve), which is why 4-bit weights usually need the finer granularity and retraining from lesson 4.

blocks.md: Misconception: int8 means the model can only represent values between -128 and 127. The integers are codes; the scale maps them to any real range. What int8 limits is the number of distinct levels (256) inside that range, so the range you pick matters more than the bit width alone.

blocks.question: An activation tensor after ReLU has range [0, 6]. Using asymmetric int8 with q_min = -128, what are S and Z?
blocks.explain: S = (6 - 0) / (127 - (-128)) = 6/255 = 0.0235, and Z = round(-128 - 0/S) = -128. Real 0 maps to the lowest code, so all 256 levels cover [0, 6]. The symmetric choice (S = 6/127, Z = 0) would waste the 128 negative codes on values ReLU never produces.

blocks.question: Why does the quantization scheme require that real 0 maps exactly to an integer code?
options: Because int8 cannot store negative numbers
Because zero padding and ReLU zeros would otherwise all carry the same rounding error, acting as a systematic bias
Because the scale S must be an integer
Because dequantization divides by zero otherwise
blocks.explain: Zero padding inserts many zeros at borders and ReLU creates many exact zeros. If 0 were not on the grid, they would all round to the same nonzero value, a biased error repeated across the tensor. Jacob et al. and the ONNX Runtime docs both call this requirement out.

lessons.title: Integer-only inference: int8 multiplies, int32 accumulators

blocks.md: Storing weights as int8 already cuts size by 4x. The bigger prize is computing in integers, since most CPUs, DSPs and NPUs process 8-bit data faster and some microcontrollers and accelerators have no fast floating point at all. Jacob et al. show that a whole layer can run with integer arithmetic only, even though the scales are real numbers.

Take a matrix product $r_3 = r_1 r_2$ where $r_1$ are weights, $r_2$ activations and $r_3$ the output, each with its own $(S_\alpha, Z_\alpha)$. Substitute $r = S(q - Z)$ into each entry and solve for the output code:

blocks.caption: Equations 4 and 5 of Jacob et al. Everything is an integer except the single constant M, known before inference.

blocks.md:
Three engineering details make this fast and exact enough:

1. **Accumulate in int32.** One product of an int8 weight and a shifted 8-bit activation can be as large as 127 x 255 = 32,385, so just two of them overflow int16 (max 32,767). The paper's inner loop is `int32 += uint8 * uint8`.
2. **Bias in int32** with scale $S_1 S_2$ and zero point 0, so it adds straight into the accumulator. It is kept wide because a bias error is added to every output and would act as a systematic shift.
3. **Requantize with a fixed-point multiplier.** $M$ is empirically in (0, 1), so write $M = 2^{-n} M_0$ with $M_0 \in [0.5, 1)$, store $M_0$ as the int32 nearest to $2^{31} M_0$, multiply, then do a rounding right shift by $n$.

blocks.title: One output of a quantized layer, step by step
blocks.code:
S1 = 0.55 / 127          # weight scale, Z1 = 0
q1 = [92, -58, 23, 127]  # int8 weights
S2, Z2 = 2.0 / 255, -128 # input range [0, 2]
q2 = [-26, -102, 63, -52]
S3, Z3 = 1.5 / 255, -128 # output range [0, 1.5]
qb = 1472                # int32 bias = round(0.05 / (S1*S2))
acc = 0                  # int32 accumulator
for j in range(4):
    acc += q1[j] * (q2[j] - Z2)
acc += qb
M0, n = 1587221510, 7    # S1*S2/S3 = (M0 / 2**31) * 2**-n
q3 = Z3 + round(acc * M0 / 2**31 / 2**n)
q3 = max(-128, min(127, q3))
y = S3 * (q3 - Z3)       # dequantize only to check

scenes.caption: Float weights [0.40, -0.25, 0.10, 0.55] become symmetric int8 with S1 = 0.55/127 = 0.00433, so 0.55 maps to 127.
Inputs [0.80, 0.20, 1.50, 0.60] use the range [0, 2] measured during calibration: S2 = 0.00784, Z2 = -128.
The output range [0, 1.5] was also calibrated. The bias 0.05 is stored as an int32 at scale S1 x S2.
Integer multiply-accumulate. After the first term the accumulator holds 92 x 102 = 9,384.
After all four terms: 9,384 - 1,508 + 4,393 + 9,652 = 21,921. No float has been touched.
Add the int32 bias: 23,393.
M = S1 S2 / S3 = 0.005774 = 0.7391 x 2^-7, so M0 = 1,587,221,510 as int32 and n = 7. acc x M = 135.08 rounds to 135, plus Z3 gives 7.
Saturate to int8 (this clamp also performs ReLU, since Z3 = -128 means real 0). Dequantized: 0.00588 x 135 = 0.794 versus the float answer 0.800, one output step away.

blocks.md: Simplified: real kernels do the multiply by $M_0$ as an integer high-multiply and the shift as an integer rounding shift, and Jacob et al. also expand the zero-point terms so the core loop is a plain integer product; the extra sums cost $O(N^2)$ against the $O(N^3)$ matrix multiply. Symmetric weights ($Z_1 = 0$) remove one of those correction terms, which is why weights are usually symmetric.

scenes.caption: 8-bit operands go in. The weights were quantized once at conversion; the input was produced by the previous int8 layer.
Products accumulate in int32 and the int32 bias is added with no rescaling, because its scale is exactly S1 x S2.
The single fixed-point multiply and shift converts to the output scale, then a saturating cast to int8 also applies ReLU or ReLU6 as a clamp.

blocks.md: LiteRT exposes this as a ladder of post-training options. **Dynamic range** quantization stores weights as int8 and quantizes activations on the fly, but outputs stay float. **Full integer** quantization also fixes activation ranges ahead of time from a **representative dataset** (the docs suggest roughly 100 to 500 samples), giving 3x or more speedup and compatibility with integer-only hardware such as microcontrollers and the Edge TPU. **Float16** halves size and suits GPUs, but is dequantized to fp32 on CPU.

blocks.code:
import tensorflow as tf

def representative_dataset():
    for x in calibration_images.take(200):   # unlabeled samples
        yield [tf.cast(x, tf.float32)]

converter = tf.lite.TFLiteConverter.from_saved_model(saved_model_dir)
converter.optimizations = [tf.lite.Optimize.DEFAULT]
converter.representative_dataset = representative_dataset
converter.target_spec.supported_ops = [tf.lite.OpsSet.TFLITE_BUILTINS_INT8]
converter.inference_input_type = tf.int8
converter.inference_output_type = tf.int8
tflite_model = converter.convert()
blocks.caption: Integer-only conversion following the LiteRT post-training quantization docs. Without the last three settings, ops with no integer kernel fall back to float, which an int8-only device cannot run.

blocks.question: A team accumulates int8 x int8 products in an int16 register to save space. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, products of 8-bit numbers always fit in 16 bits
Sums overflow: one product can reach about 32,000, so two products can already exceed the int16 maximum
The zero point can no longer be represented
The scale M stops being in (0, 1)
blocks.explain: A single product fits in 16 bits, but the dot product adds hundreds or thousands of them. Jacob et al. use an int32 accumulator for exactly this reason. ONNX Runtime documents a related saturation issue for the VPMADDUBSW instruction on AVX2 and AVX-512, where an intermediate result must fit in 16 bits and is otherwise clamped.

blocks.question: Why is the bias quantized to int32 with scale S1 x S2 instead of int8 with its own scale?
options: So it can be added directly into the int32 accumulator, and so its error does not become a systematic shift on every output
Because biases are larger than weights
Because int8 cannot represent negative biases
Because the bias is applied after dequantization to float
blocks.explain: The accumulator's scale is S1 x S2, so a bias at that scale is added with no conversion. Each bias value is added to many outputs, so any rounding error in it is a nonzero-mean error; 32 bits make it negligible, and biases are a tiny fraction of parameters.

lessons.title: Per-channel scales, calibration, and quantization-aware training

blocks.md: So far one $(S, Z)$ covered a whole tensor: **per-tensor** (or per-layer) quantization. Jacob et al. list two common failure modes of simple post-training quantization: outlier weights (lesson 2) and output channels whose weight ranges differ by more than 100x. With one shared scale, the small-range channel is crushed onto a few levels.

Toy example: a conv layer with two output channels, each with six weights. Channel 0 is tiny (max |w| = 0.021), channel 1 is large (max |w| = 2.6), a 124x range ratio. Quantize with symmetric int8, first with one scale, then with one scale per output channel (**per-channel** or per-axis).

blocks.title: int8 codes for a 2-channel weight tensor

scenes.caption: Per-tensor: S = 2.6/127 = 0.0205 for both channels. Channel 1 uses the full code range, but channel 0's weights all become -1, 0 or 1.
Per-channel: channel 0 gets its own S = 0.021/127 = 0.000165 and now spreads over -127 to 115. Channel 1 is unchanged.

blocks.title: Relative error of the dequantized weights

scenes.caption: Relative L2 error (norm of error over norm of weights). Per-tensor destroys channel 0: 38.4% error, versus 0.27% for channel 1.
Per-channel brings channel 0 down to 0.32%. The cost is one extra scale per output channel, which is negligible storage.

blocks.md: This is not a contrived case. Krishnamoorthi's whitepaper (2018) traces it to batch normalization, which rescales each output channel differently and so causes extreme range variation across the kernels of one layer. Its post-training results on ImageNet show per-tensor weight quantization collapsing MobileNets while per-channel works:

blocks.title: MobileNetV2 1.0 224, ImageNet top-1, 8-bit weights and activations

scenes.caption: Float baseline: 71.9%.
Post-training quantization (PTQ) with one asymmetric scale per weight tensor: 0.1%. The model is destroyed.
PTQ with symmetric per-channel weights: 69.8%, within about 2 points of float, matching the whitepaper's headline.
Quantization-aware training (QAT) recovers per-tensor to 70.9% and per-channel to 71.1%. Numbers from Tables 3 and 4 of Krishnamoorthi (2018).

blocks.md: The whitepaper's recommendation, which LiteRT follows, is **per-channel weights and per-tensor activations**. Activations stay per-tensor because a per-channel activation scale would complicate the inner product: each term would need its own rescale inside the accumulation.

Weights are constants, so their ranges are known. Activations depend on the input, which leaves two choices:

- **Static** quantization runs **calibration data** through the model once, records ranges, and freezes $(S, Z)$ into the file. ONNX Runtime offers MinMax, Entropy and Percentile calibration.
- **Dynamic** quantization computes activation ranges on the fly for every input. It is usually more accurate but adds runtime cost.

ONNX Runtime recommends dynamic for RNNs and transformers and static for CNNs.

When post-training quantization loses too much, **quantization-aware training (QAT)** fine-tunes the model with the rounding in the loop. Weights stay float, but the forward pass inserts **fake quantization** nodes that quantize and immediately dequantize, so the loss sees exactly the error inference will see:

blocks.tex: \hat{x} = S\Big(\mathrm{clamp}\big(\mathrm{round}(x/S) + Z,\ q_{min},\ q_{max}\big) - Z\Big), \qquad \frac{\partial \hat{x}}{\partial x} \approx \begin{cases} 1 & x_{min} \le x \le x_{max} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
blocks.caption: Rounding has zero gradient almost everywhere, so the backward pass uses the straight-through estimator: pass gradients through unchanged inside the range, block them outside.

scenes.caption: Start with post-training quantization: no retraining, only unlabeled calibration samples.
Always measure the quantized model; accuracy loss depends on the model and is hard to predict, and small models like MobileNets lose the most.
If the drop is too large, switch to QAT: fine-tune with simulated quantization on labeled data, then convert again.

blocks.md: Below 8 bits the gap widens. In the whitepaper, 4-bit weights after post-training quantization collapse many networks, while QAT brings losses to between 2% and 10% versus float, worse for smaller networks. Treat 4-bit as a QAT project.

blocks.question: A post-training int8 model loses 30 points of accuracy. Inspecting one conv layer, you find output channel ranges from 0.003 to 4.0, and the converter used one scale per tensor. What is the cheapest fix to try first?
options: Switch to quantization-aware training
Increase the calibration set from 200 to 20,000 images
Quantize activations per channel
Use per-channel weight scales
blocks.explain: A 1,300x range spread across channels is the classic per-tensor failure. Per-channel weight scales fix it with no training, and the whitepaper shows they recover MobileNetV2 to within about 2 points. More calibration data affects activation ranges, not weight ranges. QAT works too but costs a training run.

blocks.question: Why do the gradients in QAT use the straight-through estimator instead of the true derivative of round()?
options: The true derivative is zero almost everywhere, so no gradient would reach the weights
round() is not implemented on GPUs
The estimator makes training faster but changes the final model format
It removes the need for calibration
blocks.explain: round() is a step function: its derivative is zero except at the jumps, where it is undefined. Treating the quantizer as identity inside the clipping range lets gradients flow so the float weights can move to positions that quantize well.

lessons.title: Fewer operations and fewer weights, then shipping it

blocks.md: Quantization makes each number cheaper. The other lever is to need fewer numbers and fewer operations in the first place. The standard building block for this on phones and microcontrollers is the **depthwise separable convolution**, used by MobileNets.

A standard $k \times k$ convolution mixes space and channels at once: each of $d_j$ output channels looks at a $k \times k$ window over all $d_i$ input channels. The separable version splits the job in two: a **depthwise** convolution applies one $k \times k$ filter per input channel (spatial filtering only), then a **pointwise** 1x1 convolution mixes channels.

blocks.caption: Multiply-accumulates (MACs) for an h x w output, from Sandler et al. (MobileNetV2), equation 1 and its footnote.

blocks.prompt: A layer has a 56x56 output, 64 input channels, 128 output channels and 3x3 kernels. How many times fewer MACs does the separable version need?
blocks.reveal: Standard: 56 x 56 x 64 x 128 x 9 = 231.2 million MACs. Depthwise: 56 x 56 x 64 x 9 = 1.8 million. Pointwise: 56 x 56 x 64 x 128 = 25.7 million. Separable total 27.5 million, so 8.4x fewer, matching $9 \cdot 128/(9 + 128) = 8.41$. Weights drop from 73,728 to 8,768. The MobileNetV2 paper sums this up as 8 to 9 times less computation for 3x3 kernels at a small accuracy cost.

blocks.title: MACs for one 56x56, 64 to 128 channel, 3x3 layer

scenes.caption: Standard convolution: 231.2 million multiply-accumulates.
Depthwise part: 1.8 million. It is cheap because it never mixes channels.
Pointwise part: 25.7 million. Now almost all the cost is in the 1x1 channel mixing.
Total 27.5 million, 8.4x less. MobileNetV2 reaches 72.0% ImageNet top-1 with 3.4M parameters and 300M multiply-adds built from such blocks.

blocks.md: **Pruning** removes weights. Han et al. (Deep Compression, 2016) train normally, remove every connection whose weight magnitude is below a threshold, then retrain the survivors; this cut connections 9x for AlexNet and 13x for VGG-16. Combined with weight sharing (5 bits per weight) and Huffman coding, storage shrank 35x for AlexNet (240 MB to 6.9 MB) and 49x for VGG-16 (552 MB to 11.3 MB) without accuracy loss.

A pruned layer saves space only if it is stored sparsely. Deep Compression stores the nonzero values plus, for each, the index difference from the previous nonzero (8 bits for conv layers), inserting a filler zero if it does not fit. The figure stores the equivalent count of zeros skipped, the **gap**, which is that difference minus 1. Here 12 weights are pruned at threshold 0.1:

scenes.caption: Twelve trained weights. Magnitude pruning keeps only |w| of at least 0.1.
Four survive, at positions 1, 5, 8 and 11. The others become exact zeros (retraining then adjusts the survivors).
Store values and how many zeros precede each: 4 values + 4 gaps = 8 bytes at int8, versus 12 bytes dense. At 80% sparsity the same scheme gives the 10x in lesson 1.

blocks.md: Pruning does not automatically make a model smaller or faster. The LiteRT docs state that pruned models are the same size on disk and have the same latency; they only compress better. You get size savings from a sparse format or compression, and speed only from kernels or hardware that skip zeros. With 8-bit values plus 8-bit gaps, sparse storage only wins once more than half the weights are zero.

nodes.label:
measure on device:
accuracy, ms, RAM

scenes.caption: Distill a teacher into a student built from cheap blocks such as depthwise separable convolutions. This fixes the MAC and parameter count.
Optionally prune and fine-tune, if the runtime or a compression step can exploit the zeros.
Quantize: post-training first, quantization-aware training if accuracy drops too far. Then convert to the runtime's format.
Measure all three budgets on the real device, since kernel support, not the paper math, decides the final latency.

blocks.md: Each runtime packages these steps differently. **LiteRT** (formerly TensorFlow Lite) quantizes in its converter, and **LiteRT for Microcontrollers** runs the result without an operating system or dynamic allocation, in a core runtime that fits in 16 KB on a Cortex-M3. **ONNX Runtime** provides `quantize_dynamic` and `quantize_static`, can write the QDQ format (QuantizeLinear and DequantizeLinear pairs around ops), and recommends signed int8 for both activations and weights first. **ExecuTorch** uses torchao's PT2E flow with a quantizer chosen per backend:

blocks.code:
from torchao.quantization.pt2e.quantize_pt2e import prepare_pt2e, convert_pt2e

graph = torch.export.export(model, sample_inputs).module()
prepared = prepare_pt2e(graph, quantizer)   # e.g. an XNNPACKQuantizer
for sample in calibration_data:             # calibrate observers
    prepared(sample)
quantized = convert_pt2e(prepared)          # then lower to the backend
blocks.caption: The PT2E flow from the ExecuTorch quantization overview. The quantizer, not you, decides which ops and granularities the target backend supports.

blocks.md:
Common failure modes to check before shipping:

- **Float fallback.** Ops without integer kernels silently stay float, which breaks on integer-only targets.
- **Sensitive activations.** LiteRT reports DeepSpeech 0.5.1 at 6.13% character error rate in float, 43.67% with int8 activations, and 6.52% with 16-bit activations and int8 weights (its experimental 16x8 mode).
- **Small models lose most.** MobileNets are hit harder than ResNets by the same quantization scheme, so measure rather than assume.

Order of operations for edge models: pick an efficient architecture and distill into it, quantize to int8 with per-channel weights, fall back to QAT if accuracy drops, prune only when your runtime benefits, and verify accuracy, latency and peak RAM on the actual device.

blocks.question: You replace every 3x3 conv in a model with depthwise separable blocks and the MAC count drops 8x, but measured latency on your phone CPU drops only 2x. Which explanation is most plausible?
options: The MAC formula is wrong
Depthwise layers do few MACs per byte moved, so they are limited by memory traffic and kernel efficiency rather than arithmetic
Separable convolutions use more parameters
Latency always scales exactly with MACs, so the measurement must be wrong
blocks.explain: MAC counts ignore memory traffic and kernel quality. A depthwise layer does only k x k MACs per input value, so it is often bound by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic. This is why the pipeline ends with measurement on the device.

blocks.question: After magnitude pruning 50% of weights, the exported LiteRT file is exactly as large as before. What happened?
options: Pruning failed and should be repeated with a higher threshold
The zeros are still stored densely; you need compression or a sparse format to see savings
int8 quantization undid the pruning
LiteRT does not support models with zero weights
blocks.explain: A pruned dense tensor still stores every zero. The LiteRT docs say pruned models are the same size on disk and only compress better. With 8-bit values plus 8-bit gaps, sparse storage only wins once well over half the weights are zero.

blocks.question: A wake-word model meets its accuracy target in float but loses 6 points after full-integer PTQ with per-channel weights. Calibration data is representative. What should you try next?
options: Quantization-aware training, or 16-bit activations if the runtime supports them
Per-tensor weights instead of per-channel
Remove calibration and use dynamic range quantization on a microcontroller with no float unit
Prune the model to 90% sparsity
blocks.explain: Per-channel weights and good calibration are already in place, so the remaining error likely comes from activations or from a small model's sensitivity. QAT lets the model adapt to rounding, and 16x8 mode reduces activation error. Per-tensor would be worse, and dynamic range keeps float outputs that an integer-only MCU cannot run.
